hints: Think about why Sc and Zn are not counted as transition elements even though they are in the d block, focus on the ions they form.
walkthrough:
Separate d block from transition element**
Being in the d block is not enough. You are looking for the special property of the ion, not just the atom. Sc forms only $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ with $3d^0$ and Zn forms only $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ with $3d^{10}$, so neither has a partially filled d subshell in a stable ion.

Give the precise Cambridge definition**
A transition element is an element that can form at least one stable ion with incomplete 3d orbitals. The words stable ion and incomplete / partially filled are both essential for the mark.
Final answer: An element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete / partially filled 3d subshell / d orbitals.

hints: Recall how the 5 degenerate d orbitals split into two sets in a complex, and which geometry gives a large upper set of 2 and which gives a large upper set of 3.
walkthrough:
Start from degenerate**
In the isolated $\text{M}^{n+}$ ion with no ligands, all five 3d orbitals have exactly the same energy. They are degenerate. Ligands approaching split them into two levels.

Remember the opposite patterns**
In an octahedral complex the splitting is 3 lower plus 2 higher. In a tetrahedral complex it is reversed, 2 lower plus 3 higher, with a smaller energy gap. Draw both patterns clearly against the energy axis.
Final answer: Octahedral: lower level of 3 boxes and upper level of 2 boxes. Tetrahedral: lower level of 2 boxes and upper level of 3 boxes.

hints: In an octahedral complex ligands approach directly along the x, y and z axes, so think which d orbital lobes point along the axes and which point in between.
Link lower energy to less repulsion (lobes avoid ligands) and higher energy to more repulsion (lobes point at ligands).
walkthrough:
Picture ligands on the axes**
In an octahedral complex the six ligands sit on $+x, -x, +y, -y, +z, -z$. Any electron density pointing straight along an axis will be repelled strongly by a ligand lone pair.

Draw the lower set**
The $d_{xy}$, $d_{xz}$ and $d_{yz}$ orbitals have four lobes that all lie in between the axes. They feel less repulsion, so they form the lower energy $t_{2g}$ set. Sketch one clover leaf shape at 45 degrees to the axes.

Draw the higher set**
The $d_{x^2-y^2}$ has four lobes on the x and y axes, and $d_{z^2}$ has lobes on the z axis plus a torus. They point directly at ligands, feel more repulsion, and form the higher energy $e_g$ set. Sketch one of these with lobes on the axes.
Final answer: Lower energy level: any one of $d_{xy}$, $d_{xz}$, $d_{yz}$ with lobes lying between the axes. Higher energy level: $d_{z^2}$ or $d_{x^2-y^2}$ with lobes lying on / along the axes.

hints: Count how many coordinate bonds are needed to make an octahedral complex from one ligand, and look for atoms with lone pairs in $\text{edds}^{4-}$.
walkthrough:
Spot the hexadentate ligand**
The product $[\text{Fe(edds)}]^-$ is octahedral, so 6 coordinate bonds must come from one $\text{edds}^{4-}$. That means 6 donor atoms.

Identify donors with lone pairs**
The two amine N atoms each have a lone pair, and each carboxylate $\text{CO}_2^-$ donates through one O atom. So circle the 2 N atoms plus 4 O atoms, one from each carboxylate.
Final answer: Circle both N atoms and one O atom from each $\text{CO}_2^-$ group (all four $\text{O}^-$ donor atoms), total 6 donor atoms.

hints: Recall where colour in transition metal complexes comes from, promotion of an electron between the two split d levels.
Think how changing the ligand from $\text{edds}^{4-}$ to $\text{edta}^{4-}$ changes the size of the d orbital splitting and therefore the light absorbed.
walkthrough:
Recall the origin of colour**
Colour is not the ligand itself. White light shines on the complex, a d electron absorbs a photon equal to the splitting energy $\Delta E$ and jumps from the lower to the higher d set. The colour you see is the light left over.

Link ligand to splitting**
$\text{edds}^{4-}$ and $\text{edta}^{4-}$ are different ligands with different donor strengths and geometry around $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. They split the 3d orbitals by a different amount, so $\Delta E$ is different.

Link splitting to observed colour**
Since $\Delta E = h\nu$, a different gap means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed. One complex absorbs wavelengths that leave red transmitted, the other leaves yellow transmitted.

Final answer: Different ligands cause a different d-d energy gap / $\Delta E$.\nA different frequency / wavelength / energy of visible light is absorbed to promote a d electron, so a different colour is transmitted / observed.

hints: Look at what leaves and what enters the coordination sphere: six $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands are lost and one $\text{edds}^{4-}$ takes their place.
walkthrough:
Track the ligands**
Start with $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}$ where the ligands are six water molecules. End with $[\text{Fe(edds)}]^-$ where the ligand is $\text{edds}^{4-}$.

Name the type**
One ligand replaces another in the coordination sphere with no change in oxidation state of Fe. That is ligand substitution, also accepted as ligand exchange or displacement.
Final answer: Ligand exchange / substitution / displacement / replacement.

hints: Write the equilibrium law as products over reactants for the formation reaction, remembering which species is a pure liquid and is omitted.
walkthrough:
Apply the equilibrium law**
$K_{\text{stab}}$ is the equilibrium constant for formation of the complex: $[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{3+}(\text{aq}) + \text{edds}^{4-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(edds)}]^-(\text{aq}) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$. Put complex concentration on top, reactants multiplied below.

Omit water**
$\text{H}_2\text{O}(\text{l})$ is a pure liquid with effectively constant concentration, so it is left out of the expression, giving $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[\text{Fe(edds)}^-]}{[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{3+}][\text{edds}^{4-}]}$$
Final answer: $K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[\text{Fe(edds)}^-]}{[\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6^{3+}][\text{edds}^{4-}]}$

hints: Recall that a larger equilibrium constant means the formation equilibrium lies further to the right, towards the complex.
walkthrough:
Compare the numbers**
$K_{\text{stab}}$ for $[\text{Fe(edta)}]^-$ is $1.26 \times 10^{25}$ while for $[\text{Fe(edds)}]^-$ it is $3.98 \times 10^{20}$. The edta value is about $10^5$ times larger.

Translate to stability**
A larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means a greater concentration of complex relative to free metal and ligand at equilibrium, so the complex is thermodynamically more stable. Therefore $[\text{Fe(edta)}]^-$ is more stable.
Final answer: $[\text{Fe(edta)}]^-$ is more stable as it has the higher / larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ ($1.26 \times 10^{25}$ compared to $3.98 \times 10^{20}$).

hints: Notice the target equilibrium is formation of $[\text{Fe(edta)}]^-$ minus formation of $[\text{Fe(edds)}]^-$, so divide the two $K_{\text{stab}}$ values in the correct order.
walkthrough:
See Kc as Kstab ratio**
$$[\text{Fe(edds)}]^-(\text{aq}) + \text{edta}^{4-}(\text{aq}) \rightleftharpoons [\text{Fe(edta)}]^-(\text{aq}) + \text{edds}^{4-}(\text{aq})$$ This is the edta formation equilibrium divided by the edds formation equilibrium, so $$K_c = \frac{K_{\text{stab}}(\text{edta})}{K_{\text{stab}}(\text{edds})}$$

Substitute and calculate**
$$K_c = \frac{1.26 \times 10^{25}}{3.98 \times 10^{20}} = 3.17 \times 10^4$$ No units are required for this $K_c$. The large value confirms $[\text{Fe(edta)}]^-$ is favoured.
Final answer: $K_c = \dfrac{1.26 \times 10^{25}}{3.98 \times 10^{20}} = 3.17 \times 10^4$
